chapters.title: Cold open

captions.text: Say you're a photographer on an Antarctic assignment, and you've just
watched a leopard seal kill a penguin beside your boat.
The water is minus one degrees Celsius.
Your guide says get in with your camera.
You do, numb with fear. The seal is about 3.7 meters
long and weighs around 450 kilograms.
She rushes you and takes your camera, and your head, into
her mouth. It looks like a threat display, and it lasts
a few minutes. Then she relaxes, catches a penguin, stops about
three meters away, and lets it go.
It swims toward you. You can't catch it, so she tries

again.
When live penguins fail, she brings dead ones.
Four or five float around your head.
She flips them onto you, pushes you around, blows bubbles in
your face, and tries to force-feed your camera.
On the last day, a second leopard seal swims in.
She chases it off, takes its penguin, and brings it to

you.
Over four days, Paul Nicklen decided she'd concluded that he
was a useless predator who was going to starve in her

ocean. Honestly, fair.

Here's the part that doesn't add up.
In 2003, another leopard seal killed a scientist off Antarctica.
So what is this animal doing when it looks at you?
Because the more you learn about it, the less it looks
like an attack or a kindness, and the more it looks
like a test.

visual_directions: [VISUAL: first-person view under the ice edge, green-black water, a huge spotted head rising toward the camera]
[PAUSE. VISUAL: on-screen text, "Documented fatal leopard seal attacks on humans: 1"]

chapters.title: The animal

captions.text: First, the hardware. The leopard seal is the largest of the
four Antarctic seal species, and the biggest females pass three and
a half meters and five hundred kilograms.
Its jaws are wide and massive, with long curving canines for
gripping, and back teeth with three interlocking cusps that strain krill
out of the water. A murder weapon with a colander built
in. In short bursts it can reach forty kilometers an hour,
and its only natural predator is the orca.
That says plenty about the neighborhood.
Leopard seals live more than twenty-six years, mostly alone, scattered across
millions of square miles of pack ice, which makes them hard
to study and harder to predict.
But the hardware isn't what makes it dangerous.
The curiosity is.

visual_directions: [VISUAL: scale comparison, leopard seal next to a diver and a horse]

chapters.title: The menu

captions.text: Start with what's on the menu.
Anything small enough to kill. Krill is the winter staple, then
fish, squid, penguins, and the pups of other seals.
Seven penguin species are on that list, from chinstraps to emperors.
One leopard seal caught near Sydney had eaten a fully grown
platypus, which says two things: leopard seals wander, and they're not

picky.
If you're a young crabeater seal, the odds are grim.
About seventy-eight percent of crabeaters carry parallel scars consistent with escaping
a leopard seal. And if you're a newly fledged penguin, you're
the most vulnerable bird on the menu, because seals ambush you
on the way to and from the colony.
Each seal hunts her own way, too.
In 2013 and 2014, researchers strapped cameras to seven females at
Livingston Island and collected more than fifty hours of footage.
Scat studies had suggested the seals fed mostly on krill offshore.
The video showed them staying near the coast, hunting fur seal
pups and fish. Some stalked fish and flushed them from crevices.
Others chased them in open water.
And the smallest seal in the study had her meal stolen
by another leopard seal six times.
Six. Even the top of the food chain gets its lunch
taken.

visual_directions: [VISUAL: animated food web, krill to penguins to seals, red arrows toward the leopard seal]

chapters.title: The kill

captions.text: Leopard seals are ambush hunters that feed in the water, not
on land. Now say you're the penguin.
The seal catches the penguin in the water, then brings its
prey to the surface to feed.
The best place for this is the ice edge, where penguins
bunch up before they dive. In one study at Prydz Bay,
seals worked the fast-ice edge where departing Adélie penguins gathered.
Researchers saw five different hunting techniques and estimated that just six
seals could eat about two point seven percent of the adult
Adélie population over roughly 120 days.
Now look at who else stands at the ice edge.
Penguins stand upright. So do you.
The researchers' best idea is that against white ice, you look
like a dark, upright shape, and the only other thing that
stands up out there is a penguin.

visual_directions: [VISUAL: animated sequence of the thrash, then a map of the Prydz Bay ice edge]

chapters.title: Where you come in

captions.text: So what happens when you're the dark shape?
British Antarctic Survey researchers collected questionnaires from seventy people describing 137
encounters with leopard seals. The majority of attacks happened at the
ice edge, and in most of them the seal wasn't seen
beforehand. In more than half the reports from sea ice, the
seal pursued the person. In 1985, a Scottish polar explorer named
Gareth Wood was bitten on the leg by a seal that
broke through thin ice. His companions kicked it in the head
with ice crampons until it let go.

That's Antarctic first aid.
If you're thinking a boat is safer,
the seals disagree. The same study counted thirteen cases of physical
contact with small boats, including punctured rubber ones, and American researchers
have had to fit guards on their inflatables to stop the
seals from popping them.

visual_directions: [VISUAL: archival-style illustration, ice edge, a leg, a crampon]

chapters.title: The one death

captions.text: Then there's the one that changed everything.
On July 22, 2003, Kirsty Brown, a 28-year-old marine biologist with
the British Antarctic Survey, was snorkeling with her partner twenty meters
from shore at Rothera research station, studying how icebergs scour marine
life. A leopard seal held her underwater.
Her colleagues pulled her out, and the station doctor tried to
revive her for about an hour.
She was pronounced dead at 16:50.
It remains the only documented fatal leopard seal attack, and at
the time the British Antarctic Survey called it completely unprecedented.
The coroner recorded accidental death by drowning caused by a leopard
seal attack. The seal was estimated at four and a half
meters long, measured against the rescue boat, and the study's authors
concluded it was hunting, not being curious.
Ian Boyd, then director of the Sea Mammal Research Unit, offered
three explanations: it was startled and defended itself, it mistook her
for another seal, or it knew exactly what she was.
And neither the shore party nor her partner saw it coming.
Which means "just watch for it" isn't a plan.

visual_directions: [VISUAL: a quiet shot of Rothera station and the bay, no animation]

chapters.title: Reading the signals

captions.text: So how would you read one?
You can't, really. When researchers listed what leopard seals do around
people in the water, the same pattern kept coming up.
The seal approaches, often from above.
It circles in closer. It disappears from view, then reappears.
It lifts its head, shakes it, and opens and shuts its
mouth. Many observers described that as curious.
Nicklen got a few of those, and a penguin.
But the authors also flagged the possible warning signs: circling in
toward the person, approaching the head, and blowing air or bubbles.
And that open mouth? Many people read it as aggression, and
between leopard seals it's part of aggressive and defensive displays.
In other seals, an open mouth is often a sign of
submission. It might also mean the animal feels threatened, and a
threatened animal can be unpredictable. Boyd's own summary was that leopard
seals are inquisitive about people, probably sizing them up as potential
prey. So the same display can mean curious, scared, or deciding.
Which is exactly what a test looks like from the inside.

visual_directions: [VISUAL: three-panel animation, circle, head shake, open mouth, each labeled with its possible meanings]

chapters.title: Your options

captions.text: Suppose a leopard seal is circling you in the water.
As Nicklen put it, you're at the predator's mercy.

Your options?
Swim away? It reaches forty kilometers an hour, and
the researchers list moving rapidly away and turning away among the
things that can make a seal react more.
Block its path? Also on the list.
Blow bubbles at it? Also on the list.
Fight? Gareth Wood's friends did, with crampons.

Nobody recommends it.
Which leaves the dullest advice in Antarctica: stay
calm, keep facing the seal, and if things escalate, retreat slowly,
still facing it. After 2003, the British Antarctic Survey added a
thirty-minute watch for marine mammals before any dive, and banned snorkeling.
If one turns up on a beach, New Zealand's Department of
Conservation says stay at least twenty meters away and never touch
or feed it. The best defense against a leopard seal is
not being in its water in the first place.

visual_directions: [VISUAL: first-person underwater view, a dark shape circling above]

chapters.title: In the seal's defense

captions.text: To be fair to the seal, you're the one who showed
up. In that same study, dive logs covering 8,947 dives at
three Antarctic sites recorded physical contact with a leopard seal on
just four. The authors worked out about one interaction per two
hundred dives, one physical contact per twenty-two hundred, and at most
one injury per nine thousand, even assuming a quarter of all
contacts caused one. And no curious seal went on to hunt
or attack. Most of the time, it just wanted a look

at you.
There's a gentler side, too.
For months each year, male leopard seals sing underwater, for up
to thirteen hours a day. A 2025 study of twenty-six males
found they use the same five sounds in a different order
for each seal, and that the songs are about as predictable
as nursery rhymes. So the animal that swings penguins around by

the head also sings.
And the seals have the bigger problem.
They depend on sea ice for breeding and resting, and one
assessment found their habitat along the western Antarctic Peninsula has shrunk
by 21 to 28 percent. Krill declines and heavier krill fishing
could also thin out their food supply.
The last circumpolar surveys, in 1999 and 2000, counted more than
35,000, which researchers consider a substantial underestimate.

visual_directions: [VISUAL: the study's numbers as simple on-screen text, one per line]

chapters.title: Close

captions.text: Go back to that photographer, with a leopard seal's mouth around
his head. She could have done anything.
She gave him a penguin. One reading is that she saw
a predator so useless she felt sorry for him.
That's the unsettling part. It isn't aggression.
It's curiosity, and curiosity is how a predator works out what
you are: food, rival, or a project.
Most of the time, you pass the test.
You just never know which day it is.
If there's another predator you want us to investigate, tell me
in the comments. And if you want to keep going deeper,
the next video is right here.

visual_directions: [VISUAL: slow push-in on the seal's eye, the photographer's silhouette reflected in it]

approved_change.new: The seal catches the penguin in the water, then brings its prey to the surface to feed.
